title: Best Liquor for No Hangover: Clear vs. Dark Spirits, Ranked
excerpt: Which liquor gives the least hangover? A buying guide to low-congener spirits like vodka, gin, and blanco tequila, why whiskey and brandy hit harder, and why proof and price matter less than you think.
metaDescription: The best liquor for no hangover: why vodka, gin, and 100% agave tequila beat whiskey and brandy, plus honest advice on proof, price, and mixers.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** no liquor gives you no hangover. The alcohol itself (ethanol) causes most of what you feel the next morning, and every spirit on the shelf is mostly ethanol and water. But spirits are not all equal. Clear, highly distilled liquors like **vodka, gin, and 100% agave blanco tequila** carry far fewer congeners, the flavor by-products of fermentation and aging that research links to worse hangovers. Dark, aged, and fruit-based liquors like **bourbon, brandy, cognac, and dark rum** carry the most. If you're standing in a liquor store trying to pick a bottle for a night out, choosing from the clear end of the shelf is a reasonable way to take the edge off the morning. It won't save you from drinking too much.

**The quick rules for buying:**

- **Best bets:** plain, unflavored vodka; a classic London Dry gin; a blanco tequila labeled **"100% de agave"**.
- **Middle of the pack:** white rum, reposado tequila, lighter Scotch and Irish whiskey.
- **Hardest on the morning:** bourbon and American whiskey, dark and spiced rum, brandy, cognac, and fruit brandies.
- **Skip regardless of category:** sugary flavored spirits, "mixto" gold tequila, cheap liqueurs, and anything homemade, unlabeled, or suspiciously cheap.
- **Price:** a decent mid-range bottle from a well-known producer is fine. Paying more buys flavor, not a better morning.
- **Proof:** stick to standard 80 proof (40% alcohol). Higher-proof bottles pack more alcohol into each pour.

> **A quick note on safety.** This is a guide to choosing a bottle and drinking it sensibly. It isn't medical advice. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has cold or bluish skin, or has a seizure. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover, so don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." See our guide to [alcohol poisoning signs](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs). Also seek urgent help for blurred vision or severe stomach pain after drinking homemade or unlabeled spirits, which can mean methanol poisoning. If you're pregnant, take medication that interacts with alcohol, or have been advised not to drink, no bottle on this list is a safe choice for you; follow your doctor's advice.

## Why the Bottle You Pick Changes the Morning (a Little)

A hangover has several causes stacked on top of each other: the alcohol itself, poor sleep, dehydration, irritation of the stomach, inflammation, and the build-up of acetaldehyde, a toxic chemical your liver makes while breaking alcohol down. Most of that comes from the amount of ethanol you drink, and the type of liquor can't change it.

What the type of liquor *can* change is the **congener load**. Congeners are the small amounts of other chemicals that end up in a drink alongside ethanol. They include methanol, fusel oils (heavier alcohols), acetaldehyde, esters, and tannins. They're a big part of why bourbon tastes like bourbon and cognac tastes like cognac. They're also, according to the research we have, one reason darker drinks seem to cause worse hangovers at the same amount of alcohol. Our full explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes deeper into what each one is and where it comes from.

Three steps in making a spirit decide how many congeners end up in your glass:

1. **What it's made from.** Grain, potatoes, and agave make fewer of some congeners than fruit. Fruit brings pectin, which breaks down into methanol during fermentation, so fruit brandies tend to have more methanol than grain spirits.
2. **How hard it's distilled.** Distillation separates ethanol from everything else. The more times and the more tightly a spirit is distilled, the more congeners get left behind. Vodka is distilled to a very high strength before being diluted, which strips out most of them. Bourbon is legally capped at a much lower distillation strength precisely so it *keeps* its flavor compounds.
3. **How long it's aged and in what.** Years in a charred oak barrel add color, tannins, and many more flavor compounds. That's why aged versions of almost any spirit carry more congeners than unaged ones.

So a simple rule works surprisingly well at the store: **the more neutral, clear, and unaged a spirit is, the fewer congeners it tends to have.** The darker, older, and more fruit-forward, the more it tends to have.

## What the Research Actually Shows

This is a smaller research area than you might expect, so it's worth being clear about what's solid and what isn't.

The best direct test is a 2010 study led by Damaris Rohsenow and published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*. Healthy young adults drank bourbon, vodka, or a placebo on different nights in a sleep lab, with the amounts set so everyone reached a similar blood alcohol level. People reported **worse hangovers after bourbon than after vodka**. But both drinks hurt sleep compared with placebo, and next-day thinking and reaction time were impaired about equally by both. In other words, the bourbon made people *feel* worse, while the alcohol itself did most of the damage either way.

Older and smaller studies point in the same direction. A 1970 bourbon-versus-vodka study by Chapman reported more hangover symptoms after bourbon, and work by G. L. S. Pawan in the early 1970s is the source of the often-repeated ranking that puts brandy near the top for hangovers and vodka and gin near the bottom. Those studies are thin by modern standards, so treat them as supporting evidence, not precise measurements. Review articles on hangover causes, including Swift and Davidson's 1998 review, list congeners as one contributing factor among several, not the main driver.

What's **not** well studied: head-to-head comparisons of individual brands, the effect of filtering methods, "triple distilled" marketing claims, or whether expensive bottles cause milder hangovers than cheap ones. Nobody has good controlled data on those. Anyone ranking specific brands by hangover is guessing.

## The Buying Ranking: Lightest to Heaviest Hangover

This ranking assumes the same amount of alcohol in each case. It's based on typical congener levels and the research above. Individual bottles vary, and so do people. For a version that includes beer and wine, see our [least hangover alcohol ranking](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).

| Rank | Liquor | Congener level | What to buy | What to avoid |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Vodka | Very low | Plain, unflavored, from a reputable producer | Sweet flavored vodkas, unlabeled or bargain-bin bottles |
| 2 | Gin | Low | Classic London Dry style | Sweetened "pink" gins and gin liqueurs |
| 3 | Blanco tequila | Low to moderate | Labeled "100% de agave", additive-free producers | "Mixto" gold tequila (only 51% agave) |
| 4 | White rum | Low to moderate | Unaged or lightly filtered white rum | Flavored and coconut rums |
| 5 | Reposado tequila | Moderate | 100% agave, lightly aged | Heavily sweetened or flavored bottles |
| 6 | Scotch and Irish whiskey | Moderate to high | Lighter blends if you want whiskey | Very heavily peated or cask-strength pours |
| 7 | Añejo tequila and aged rum | High | If you love it, drink less of it | Spiced rum with added sugar |
| 8 | Bourbon and American whiskey | High | Standard-proof bottles, small pours | Barrel-proof bottles |
| 9 | Brandy, cognac, fruit brandies | Highest | Small amounts, sipped | Cheap fruit brandies and homemade spirits |

A few notes on reading this table. The gap between rank 1 and rank 9 is real but modest: in the controlled research, switching from bourbon to vodka made hangovers milder, not absent. And the gap between drinking three drinks and six drinks is much bigger than the gap between any two rows.

## Vodka: The Cleanest Pour on the Shelf

Vodka sits at the top of almost every low-hangover list for a simple reason. It's made to be neutral. In the US, vodka is distilled to a very high strength so that most of the flavor compounds are stripped out, then diluted with water to bottling strength. What's left is about as close to plain ethanol and water as a drink gets.

**What to buy:** a plain, unflavored vodka from a well-known producer. You don't need the most expensive bottle. Once a vodka is properly made, paying more mostly buys smoother taste and nicer packaging. Grain versus potato versus grape makes little practical difference to congener levels in a properly distilled vodka.

**What to skip:** heavily sweetened flavored vodkas (the sugar and flavorings undo some of the advantage and make it easy to drink faster), and very cheap bottles from producers you've never heard of.

**The catch:** vodka has so little taste that it goes down easily, which makes it easy to drink more than you planned. A clean spirit you drink twice as much of is not a win.

Our [best vodka for no hangover](/never-hungover/best-vodka-for-no-hangover) guide covers brands, filtration claims, and mixers in detail, and our [vodka hangover guide](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) explains why vodka still causes hangovers at all.

## Gin: Nearly as Clean, With Flavor Added After

Gin starts as a neutral spirit much like vodka. The juniper and other botanicals are added by redistilling or steeping, which brings flavor without adding the barrel-aged congeners that make dark spirits rough. That's why gin usually lands just behind vodka in congener rankings.

**What to buy:** a classic London Dry gin, which by definition can't have sugar added after distillation. That keeps it dry and simple.

**What to skip:** sweetened "pink" or fruit gins and gin liqueurs, which are often bottled at lower strength with added sugar. Also watch the mixer. A gin and tonic sounds light, but regular tonic water is sugary. Diet or "light" tonic, or soda water with lime, keeps it cleaner. For more on this, see our [gin hangover guide](/never-hungover/gin-hangover).

## Blanco Tequila: Great Choice, If You Read the Label

Tequila is the category where the bottle you pick matters most, because quality varies so much. A **blanco** (also called silver or plata) tequila is unaged or rested only briefly, so it carries fewer barrel-derived congeners than aged tequilas. Many drinkers swear tequila gives them a gentler morning. There's no good controlled evidence that tequila is special in that way, but a clean blanco is a perfectly sensible low-congener choice.

**What to buy:** a bottle that says **"100% de agave"** (or "100% agave") on the label. If it doesn't say that, it's a "mixto," which only has to be 51% agave sugars, with the rest from other sugars. Mixtos are often the cheap gold tequilas behind many bad tequila nights. Mexican rules also allow small amounts of additives such as caramel coloring, glycerin, oak extract, and sweetener syrup in tequila without listing them on the label, so some drinkers check independent "additive-free" lists before buying.

**What to skip:** gold mixto tequila, pre-made margarita mixes, and heavily flavored tequilas.

Our [best tequila for no hangover](/never-hungover/best-tequila-for-no-hangover) guide explains how to read a tequila label and find additive-free producers. If you're torn between the two clear favorites, see [vodka vs. tequila hangover](/never-hungover/vodka-vs-tequila-hangover).

## White Rum: A Reasonable Middle Option

Rum is made from sugarcane or molasses, and its congener level depends heavily on style. White rum is usually unaged or aged briefly and then filtered to remove color, which also removes some congeners. It sits a step behind vodka and gin. Dark and spiced rums are a different story: longer aging, added caramel, and in spiced rums, added sugar and flavorings put them near the heavy end of the list.

**What to buy:** a straightforward white rum for mixed drinks. **What to skip:** spiced, flavored, and coconut rums if hangovers are your main concern. Our [rum hangover guide](/never-hungover/rum-hangover) covers the differences between styles.

## Whiskey and Bourbon: Why They're Near the Bottom

This is the part whiskey lovers don't want to hear. Bourbon is the drink that came out worse than vodka in the best controlled study we have, and there's a clear reason. By law, bourbon is distilled to a lower strength than vodka and aged in new charred oak barrels, both of which are designed to keep and add flavor compounds. That flavor is the point of whiskey, and congeners are a big part of it.

Scotch and Irish whiskey vary widely. Lighter blended whiskies are generally gentler than heavily aged, cask-strength, or intensely flavored bottles, but there's no good research ranking them against each other.

**If you love whiskey:** you don't have to give it up for a hangover guide. Choose a standard-proof bottle (around 80 to 90 proof), drink it slowly, add water or ice, and have fewer of them. Two well-made whiskies sipped over an evening will usually leave you better off than six vodka sodas. Our [whiskey hangover guide](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) has more.

## Brandy and Cognac: The Heaviest Hitters

Brandy, cognac, armagnac, and fruit brandies tend to sit at the very bottom of hangover rankings. They combine two congener sources: fruit (which brings more methanol, since fruit contains pectin) and long barrel aging (which adds tannins and other compounds). The older research that ranked drinks by hangover consistently put brandy at or near the top for symptoms.

These are sipping spirits for a reason. If you drink them, keep the pours small and the count low. And never drink homemade fruit brandy or unlabeled spirits of unknown origin. Poorly made fruit spirits can contain dangerous amounts of methanol, which is a poisoning risk, not just a hangover risk.

## Does Price or Quality Matter?

Partly. Here's an honest breakdown.

- **Within vodka and gin:** once a spirit is made properly by a reputable producer, price makes little difference to congeners. A mid-range bottle is fine. Very cheap, unbranded bottles are the main ones worth avoiding, mostly because you know less about how they were made.
- **Within tequila:** quality matters a lot, but it's about the label, not the price tag. "100% de agave" from a producer that doesn't use additives is the thing to look for. Some affordable bottles meet that bar, and some expensive ones don't.
- **Within whiskey, rum, and brandy:** more expensive often means older, and older usually means *more* congeners, not fewer. A pricey 18-year-old whiskey is not a hangover-friendly choice.
- **"Smooth" isn't the same as "clean."** Many cheap spirits taste smooth because of added sugar or glycerin. Smoothness makes a drink easier to drink fast, which works against you.

The marketing claims to be most skeptical of: "triple distilled" or "ten times filtered" promises of no hangover, "gluten-free means no hangover," and "organic means no hangover." None of these has good evidence behind it as a hangover fix. A well-made spirit is a modest advantage. It's never a guarantee.

## Proof Matters More Than People Think

Most people compare liquors without looking at the strength on the label, but it changes how much alcohol you get per pour.

- **Standard proof** is 80 (40% alcohol by volume). That's what a standard drink calculation assumes for a 1.5-ounce shot.
- **Higher-proof bottles** (100 proof, "navy strength" gin, barrel-proof bourbon, overproof rum) can be 50% to 65% alcohol or more. The same pour delivers a lot more ethanol, so you effectively have extra drinks without noticing.
- **Concentrated drinks hit faster.** Strong drinks taken as shots can raise blood alcohol quickly. Mixing a spirit with a non-sugary mixer and sipping it slows things down.

When you're shopping with hangovers in mind, the best bottle is usually a standard-proof one. If you do buy something stronger, pour smaller or add more water.

## The Mixer Can Cancel Out a Good Bottle

A clean vodka mixed with an energy drink or a sugary premix isn't a clean drink anymore. Sugary mixers make drinks taste less like alcohol so they go down faster, and caffeine-heavy mixers can mask how drunk you feel and make sleep worse. Both work against you the next day.

Good mixers for a clear spirit: soda water, fresh lime or lemon, a splash of plain juice, or diet tonic. Our guide to the [best mixers to avoid a hangover](/never-hungover/best-mixers-to-avoid-hangover) goes through the options.

## What Actually Moves the Needle the Next Morning

Choosing a low-congener liquor is one of the smaller levers you have. In rough order of impact, here's what matters:

1. **How much you drink.** By far the biggest factor. Fewer drinks means a milder morning, whatever's in the glass.
2. **How fast you drink.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, though this varies by person. Pacing yourself near that rate keeps blood alcohol lower.
3. **Eating first.** Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption.
4. **Water between drinks.** It slows your drinking and helps with dehydration, even if it doesn't fix the hangover by itself.
5. **Sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep, and poor sleep makes the next day much worse. Leave time to sleep it off properly.
6. **What you drink.** Clear and unaged over dark and aged, standard proof over overproof, simple mixers over sugary ones.

Mixing drinks isn't the problem people think it is, either. The "beer before liquor" rhyme doesn't hold up, and what counts is the total amount of alcohol. See [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) for the research. For the full set of habits with the best evidence, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) is the place to start.

If you find hangovers are hitting you much harder than they used to, or harder than your friends, our article on [why you get hangovers so easily](/never-hungover/why-do-i-get-hangovers-so-easily) looks at age, genetics, and other factors.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people pair a sensible drink choice with a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. The evidence is promising but limited. A widely cited 2012 study in rats (Shen and colleagues, *Journal of Neuroscience*) found DHM reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal, and lab studies suggest it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde. Human evidence is still thin, and there's no good evidence that any supplement prevents a hangover if you drink heavily.

If you want to try it alongside the habits above, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds L-cysteine and electrolytes, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Check with your doctor or pharmacist first if you take regular medication. And keep expectations honest: DHM is a possible extra, not permission to drink more.

## A Simple Shopping Plan for Your Next Night Out

If you just want a decision, here it is:

- **For mixed drinks:** a plain, standard-proof vodka from a well-known producer, with soda water and fresh citrus.
- **If you prefer flavor:** a London Dry gin with diet tonic or soda, or a 100% agave blanco tequila with soda and lime.
- **If you only drink whiskey or brown spirits:** keep it, but go standard proof, add water, sip slowly, and cut the count by a drink or two.
- **For a party where people drink fast:** buy clear spirits and good non-sugary mixers, put out plenty of water, and make sure there's food.

## The Bottom Line

The best liquor for a lighter hangover is a clear, unflavored, standard-proof spirit from a reputable producer: vodka first, then gin and 100% agave blanco tequila. The worst are bourbon, dark and spiced rum, brandy, and cognac, because aging and fruit add the congeners that research links to rougher mornings. Price matters less than the label, and for aged spirits, more expensive usually means more congeners. Above all, the type of liquor is the smaller lever. How much and how fast you drink decide most of how you'll feel tomorrow.

If whiskey is your drink, our guide to the [best whiskey for no hangover](/never-hungover/best-whiskey-for-no-hangover) goes style by style, from Irish and Scotch to bourbon and rye.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best liquor for no hangover?**

No liquor prevents a hangover, because the alcohol itself causes most of the symptoms. The liquors linked to the mildest hangovers are clear, unflavored, highly distilled spirits: vodka first, then gin and 100% agave blanco tequila. They contain far fewer congeners than dark spirits. How much and how fast you drink still matters much more than which bottle you choose.

**Which liquor gives the worst hangover?**

Brandy, cognac, bourbon, and dark or spiced rum tend to cause the worst hangovers at the same amount of alcohol. Aging in barrels and fruit-based ingredients add congeners, including more methanol in fruit brandies. In the best controlled study, bourbon produced worse hangovers than vodka at matched blood alcohol levels.

**Does expensive liquor cause less of a hangover?**

Not reliably. For vodka and gin, a mid-range bottle from a reputable producer is about as clean as a premium one. For tequila, the label matters more than price: look for 100% de agave. For whiskey, rum, and brandy, more expensive often means older, and older usually means more congeners, not fewer.

**Is tequila better than vodka for hangovers?**

Plain vodka usually has the fewest congeners of any spirit, so on paper it is the cleanest. A 100% agave blanco tequila is also a low-congener choice and close behind. There's no good controlled evidence that tequila is uniquely hangover-friendly. Cheap mixto gold tequila, which is only 51% agave, is a much worse pick than either.

**Does higher proof liquor cause a worse hangover?**

Higher-proof liquor packs more alcohol into each pour, so the same size drink gives you more ethanol, and more ethanol means a worse hangover. Strong drinks taken as shots can also raise blood alcohol quickly. Stick with standard 80 proof spirits, or pour smaller and add water if you buy something stronger.

**Are clear liquors always better than dark liquors?**

Usually, but not always. Clear and unaged spirits tend to have fewer congeners than dark and aged ones. But a sugary flavored vodka or a clear liqueur can be worse than a well-made whiskey sipped slowly. Color is a useful shortcut, not a rule, and the amount you drink outweighs it.

**Does the mixer matter if I choose a clean liquor?**

Yes. Sugary mixers and premixes make drinks easier to drink fast, and energy drinks can mask how drunk you feel and hurt your sleep. Soda water, fresh citrus, a splash of plain juice, or diet tonic keep a clear spirit simple.

**Can DHM stop a hangover from liquor?**

There's no good evidence that DHM or any supplement prevents a hangover if you drink heavily. DHM has promising research, mostly in animals and lab studies, on how the body handles alcohol, with limited human data. It can be an extra alongside drinking less and pacing yourself, not a replacement. Check with a doctor or pharmacist if you take regular medication.
